lesson.title: One Dot, One Data Point: Reading a Dotplot
lesson.summary: A dotplot shows the distribution of a quantitative variable by stacking one dot per data value above a number line, preserving every individual value while still revealing the overall pattern.
lesson.body:
A dotplot displays the distribution of a quantitative variable by drawing a horizontal number line covering the range of the data, then placing one dot above the number line for every individual data value. When two or more individuals share the same value, their dots stack directly on top of each other, so the height of a stack of dots at any point on the number line shows the frequency of that value, similar to a bar graph but built from a numeric scale rather than separate categories.

What makes a dotplot especially valuable, particularly for small data sets, is that it does not lose any information the way a frequency table grouped into wide classes can. Every single data point is represented by its own dot, so you can look at a dotplot and, in principle, read every original value back out of the picture, while also instantly seeing the overall pattern, the distribution, that those values form.

Consider the number of pets owned by 12 students: 0, 1, 1, 2, 0, 3, 1, 2, 1, 0, 2, 1. Counting how many times each value appears: 0 appears 3 times, 1 appears 5 times, 2 appears 3 times, and 3 appears once, and these counts total 3 plus 5 plus 3 plus 1, which equals 12, matching all 12 students. A dotplot of this data would show a number line from 0 to 3, with a stack of 3 dots above 0, a taller stack of 5 dots above 1, a stack of 3 dots above 2, and a single dot above 3.

Reading this dotplot tells a clear story without needing any table at all. The tallest stack sits above 1, showing that owning exactly one pet is the most common situation among these students. The values spread from a low of 0 to a high of 3, and the single dot above 3 stands somewhat apart from the rest, worth a second look as a possible unusual value. These are exactly the kinds of features, where the data clusters, how far it spreads, and whether anything looks unusual, that the shape of a distribution, covered later in this course, is built to describe precisely.

Dotplots work best when a data set is fairly small and takes on a limited number of distinct values, since a data set with hundreds of individuals and many different numeric values would produce an unwieldy chart with an impractical number of columns. For larger or more spread out quantitative data sets, a stemplot or a histogram, both covered next, offers a more practical way to organize the same kind of information while still preserving the essential shape of the distribution.

A dotplot also makes the mode, meaning the most frequently occurring value, immediately visible as the tallest stack of dots, without requiring any separate calculation. Comparing two dotplots side by side, for example the pet counts of a second group of 12 students placed on a matching number line, gives a quick visual way to judge whether one group tends toward higher or lower values than the other, whether one group is more spread out, and whether the two groups share a similar overall shape, all before calculating any formal numerical summary such as a mean or standard deviation.
